newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels say Chinese troops fly in to prop up Mobutu.
newsitem.headline: Rebels say Chinese troops fly in to prop up Mobutu.

text.p: Zairean rebels said late on Monday that 400 Chinese troops had flown into the capital Kinshasa to bolster the regime of President Mobutu Sese Seko.

A top official of Laurent Kabila's rebel movement also warned that the rebels, who said they were only days away from taking the capital, would not tolerate foreign troops on the soil of the vast central African country -- even American, Belgian or French soldiers who might be sent in to evacuate Westerners.

Mwana Nanga Mawanpanga, the rebels' choice for finance minister, said the West should "persuade Mobutu to quit" and this was the way to protect expatriates in the country, at least half of which is now in rebel control.
Reading a statement from Kabila, he said the alliance had "learned of the arrival of large contingents of Chinese troops in Kinshasa. We know of 400 troops at present".
He had "no clue" where the Chinese troops had come from, Mawanpanga told a news conference in Lubumbashi, Zaire's rebel-held second city.
"If the Chinese government did not send these troops, they can respond by a declaration. If they do not -- they may have been sent by the Chinese government," he said.
There was no immediate response from Kinshasa on the rebel report of the arrival of Chinese troops.
The warning against foreign troops appeared to be aimed at averting an evacuation initiative by Western countries with nationals in Zaire that the rebels regard as unnecessary.

Kabila has insisted that what many expect would be a bloody battle for Kinshasa can be avoided if sufficient international pressure is brought on Mobutu to realise that his rule is over and he must step aside for the good of the country.
"We will not accept any foreign soldiers on our soil, even under the pretext of evacuation," Mawanpanga said.

Asked if this included U.S., French and Belgian troops currently stationed across the Zaire river from Kinshasa in Brazzaville, capital of the Congo, he said the rebels "will not accept any foreign troops under any excuse, because this does not hold water".

"The only way to protect expatriates in Kinshasa is to persuade Mobutu to quit. They did this with (former Philippine President Ferdinand) Marcos, the Shah (of Iran) and (former Haitian leader Raoul) Phedras. They know where the evil is. They can do it (remove Mobutu)," he said.
"They can bomb his palace -- the guy will chicken out."
Asked how close rebel forces were to Kinshasa, he replied: "They are very close, very close to Kinshasa." It would be only a "matter of days" before rebel forces captured the city.
"The United States has the means to push Mobutu out of Kinshasa...they do not need to risk the lives of their soldiers," Mawanpanga said.
He reiterated that Kabila was ready to see Mobutu at any time to negotiate his departure, although not in Brazzaville.
"They know where we are willing to go," he said.

Mobutu's son and spokesman said on Monday that his father, 66 and still recovering from prostate cancer surgery, would not make the long flight to South Africa this week for a much-expected meeting with Kabila.
